Ālaya ♦ 7

'Āgama' with reference to temple deals with the temple-
building activities as well as the procedures of worship
in temples. The former appears to emphasize aesthetics,
while the latter the spiritual aspect. But the distinction
between them is arbitrary and unreal, for Beauty and
Serenity cannot in fact be separated.

There are doctrinal formulations in Āgama regarding
the selection of proper land for the temple, the purificatory
ceremonies prior to the construction, the plan 'lay-out',
direction, size, relative proportions of the plinth and other
structural parts, permissible decorations and
embellishments, installation of icons and deities in the
sanctum as well as in the niches and pavilions, rituals of
daily worship and periodical festivals, purifications and
sacramental activities, and so on. These formulations take
manifestations and content of the symbol as two
complementary elements.

The temple as an incarnation of the symbol is the
medium of rituals. Ritual is active thought. Rituals are
actions that lead to contemplation, and contemplation
strives to achieve the serenity of consciousness that lifts
one from the stress of common life. The Āgama focuses
attention on the temple as a pattern of rituals. It provides
us with a perspective to understand the symbol and act
effectively with regard to it. It seeks to construct for us
a half-way house between the limitations that we have and
the perfection we aim at. Limitations are inherent in
human life; we live amidst what pass for the commonplace
and the ugly. Perfection is a divine quality; it is also
beautiful. The purpose of rituals is to facilitate the passage
from the commonplace to the unique, from ugliness to
beauty, from what is human to what may be divine.

8 ♦ The Āgama Encyclopaedia

The Āgama had an earlier oral tradition, communicated
through generations of craftsmen and priests. It has also
a later written tradition, consisting of hundreds of texts
and manuals meant for craftsmen and priests. The oral
tradition has almost disappeared, for craftsmen as well as
priests have fallen on decadent days. The texts and
manuals have, for the same reason, gone into oblivion,
neglected by those for whom they were meant and ignored
by others in the community. Fortunately, however, many
of these literary works are available, mostly in manuscripts
and some of them in print. The literary tradition comprises
of works that are usually classified into three classes:
revelations (divya), composition of sages (muni-prokta)
and writings of ordinary men (pauruśa). The revealed
texts claim a hoary antiquity and have been relied upon
by the other two classes of works. The compositions of
sages are original works, based on inspiration, intuition
and contemplation. They now exist only in citations and
fragments. The third group of works is largely in the
nature of compilations of relevant passages from the
compositions of sages. They employ intelligence and
reason, and are also liable to err. They are chronologically
recent, and some of them are what the priests and
craftsmen mostly have relied upon for several generations
now.

The fundamental assumption in this mixed tradition is
that Divinity has two aspects: the hidden and pervasive
aspect (niṣkala), and the manifest and specific aspect
(sakala). The former is abstract and is likened to oil in
the seasasum seeds, fire in fuel, butter in milk, and scent

summary: This introduction defines 'Āgama' as the doctrinal tradition governing both temple construction (aesthetics) and worship procedures (spirituality), arguing that these two facets are inseparable. It details the comprehensive scope of Āgamic formulations, from land selection to daily rituals. The text presents the temple as a symbol and a medium for rituals, which are described as 'active thought' designed to elevate consciousness from the mundane and ugly to the beautiful and divine. It then traces the transmission of Āgamic knowledge from a now-faded oral tradition to a vast, though often neglected, written tradition. This literary corpus is categorized into three classes: divine revelations (divya), compositions of sages (muni-prokta), and writings of ordinary men (pauruśa). Finally, it introduces the core metaphysical concept of a dual-aspected Divinity: the formless, pervasive 'niṣkala' aspect and the manifest, specific 'sakala' aspect.
key_themes: The scope and definition of Āgama
The synthesis of aesthetics (Beauty) and spirituality (Serenity) in temple traditions
The role of the temple as a symbol and medium for ritual
Ritual as a transformative process from the human to the divine
The transmission of knowledge from oral to written traditions
Classification of Āgamic texts based on their origin and authority
The dual nature of Divinity: formless (niṣkala) and manifest (sakala)
main_arguments: The distinction between the aesthetic (temple-building) and spiritual (worship) aspects of Āgama is artificial and unreal, as 'Beauty and Serenity cannot in fact be separated.'
Rituals are not merely procedural actions but are a form of 'active thought' that facilitates a transition from a state of human limitation to one of divine perfection.
The Āgama tradition is preserved in a three-tiered literary corpus of varying authority (divine, sagely, human), which has largely superseded a declining oral tradition.
A foundational concept in the Āgamic tradition is that Divinity possesses two aspects: a hidden, all-pervasive, formless aspect (niṣkala) and a manifest, specific aspect (sakala).
methodology: The methodology is primarily descriptive, conceptual, and historical. It defines key terms ('Āgama', 'Ritual', 'niṣkala', 'sakala') and explains the philosophical framework underpinning the temple tradition. It employs a classificatory approach by categorizing Āgamic literary works into three types (divya, muni-prokta, pauruśa). The historical dimension is evident in its discussion of the shift from an oral to a written tradition and the current state of these traditions.
historiographical_context: The text situates the study of Āgama within a historical context of decline and preservation. It notes that the original oral tradition has 'almost disappeared' and that even the later written texts have 'gone into oblivion' due to the 'decadent days' of their practitioners (craftsmen and priests). This frames the work as an effort to recover and explain a neglected body of knowledge, relying on surviving manuscripts and printed texts as the primary source material for a tradition that has lost its direct, living lineage.
research_questions: What is the full scope of 'Āgama' in relation to Hindu temples, encompassing both its practical and philosophical dimensions?
What is the purpose of the temple and its associated rituals according to Āgamic doctrine?
How has Āgamic knowledge been transmitted and categorized, and what is the nature and authority of its source texts?
What are the fundamental metaphysical assumptions, particularly regarding the nature of Divinity, that underpin the Āgamic worldview?
book_structure_overview: This introduction lays the groundwork for a comprehensive exploration of the Āgama tradition. It establishes the core topics to be discussed: the integrated principles of temple architecture and worship, the philosophy and function of rituals, the history and classification of Āgamic texts, and the core theological concepts like the dual aspects of Divinity (niṣkala and sakala). This suggests the subsequent chapters will likely elaborate on each of these areas in greater detail, providing specific examples from the textual traditions it introduces.
